It is not often one of the new-build generation of English football stadiums has more character than a club’s former ground but the Gtech Community Stadium is a happy exception.

Griffin Park was much beloved, of course, and its peculiar feature of boasting a pub at each of the four corners of the ground was part of the game’s folklore. But Brentford pulled off an architectural wonder with the Gtech, squeezing it into a parcel of land in the shadow of the raised section of the M4 in west London.

The club has frequently had one of the best home records in the Premier League since coming up in 2021, which is testimony not just to the excellence of the players and manager but to the tight confines of the ground and the atmosphere it creates.

It is no surprise it is attracting supporters who previously considered themselves without an affiliation. It is the type of stadium, and club, that makes fans feel they belong.

Division: Championship Opened: 1801 Capacity: 10,500

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of Wrexham with distaste

I went to a lot of games in Wrexham in the late 70s and early 80s. My best mate, Bryn, was from the town so when his mum and dad took him to visit family there, I went along and we headed for the Racecourse Ground.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of the club with distaste, although I am aware that my friend and colleague Ian Herbert, a Wrexham fan and a club scholar, has had some misgivings.

Nothing in football is ever quite as wholesome as it seems but so far, it feels as if it has been good for the club and for the town.

I don’t know what their long-term motives are but they have poured a lot of money into the team and into the infrastructure, and the club has risen and risen through the leagues. It’s bringing more light into a community that has had its share of hard times.

I was at the Racecourse, by the way, when Mark Hughes scored his spectacular overhead kick against Spain in 1985. It’s still one of the top five goals I’ve ever seen live.

(The others: Angel Di Maria for Argentina at the Lusail Stadium in the 2022 World Cup final, Zlatan Ibrahimovic for Sweden against England at the Friends Arena in 2012, Dennis Bergkamp for the Netherlands against Argentina at the Stade Velodrome at France '98 and Norman Whiteside for Manchester United against Everton at Wembley in the 1985 FA Cup final)

Division: Championship Opened: 1906 Capacity: 29,409

There are wealthy owners at Birmingham now, of course, and big plans, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything

Down the winding stairs from the press box, though the main reception area where staff are trying to sort ticket requests, through the foyer, down another set of steps and into a tunnel below the Main Stand where four garden forks hang on the wall outside the groundsman’s room – St Andrew’s is still a beautiful stadium that mixes old-school elements and modern stands.

It’s a great place to watch a game. If it gets overshadowed by Aston Villa and West Brom, it still feels as if the soul of the Second City is alive in this place.

There are wealthy owners now, of course, and big plans, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1997 Capacity: 48,095

Sunderland have some of the best supporters in the country and the noise the fans make when the biggest occasions present themselves is up there with anyone

I loved Roker Park. Like Maine Road, I’d have it in my top 10 grounds if Sunderland were still playing there now and I feel lucky to have stood in the away end there and been treated to the full force of the Roker Roar.

I’ve never been quite sure what to make of its successor, the Stadium of Light. I’m not even sure about the name, which is dramatic, certainly, but is also an obvious copy of the original Benfica ground in Lisbon – which opened in 1954 and held 130,000 at its peak.

The design is rather uninspiring for such an evocative name, too. It’s uncomfortably close to identikit new-build, but I have friends who say it’s their favourite anywhere.

The stadium does sit proudly atop the bluffs of the River Wear and it’s wonderful to see the team on the up again and back in the Premier League. These are some of the best supporters in the country and the noise the fans make when the biggest occasions present themselves is up there with anyone.

Division: Championship Opened: 1855 Capacity: 32,050

Bramall Lane's Kop singing the Greasy Chip Butty song is one of the iconic experiences in English football

Bramall Lane is still the only ground where I’ve sat in the dugout during a league game.

Neil Warnock is a friend of mine and when he was in charge at Sheffield United, he let me sit next to him in an end-of-season Championship game against Ipswich Town. I got a front row seat for Rob Kozluk, one of the game’s great sledgers, doing his best to wind up then-Ipswich boss Joe Royle.

I can’t think of many better grounds to have had the privilege. Bramall Lane is a cauldron of noise, full of history and passion, in the heart of the city.

Its Kop singing the Greasy Chip Butty song is one of the iconic experiences in English football.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1877 Capacity: 40,044

All stadiums change and modernise with the years but there are few stadiums which have changed as dramatically as Stamford Bridge

All stadiums change and modernise with the years but there are few stadiums which have changed as dramatically as Stamford Bridge.

It was once an intimidating place, dominated by the Shed, a sprawling, boisterous semi-circular terrace behind one of the goals that was synonymous with the crowd problems of the 1970s and early 80s.

Going to watch a Chelsea game now is an entirely different experience. The transformation began under Ken Bates, one of a group of visionary businessmen who changed the way we watch football, and then continued under Roman Abramovich.

And now, for many, going to Chelsea, with its towering West Stand and opulent corporate boxes, is a boutique experience not out of place with the hugely affluent area in which it stands.

You can still feel the history of the place when you visit, though. To its credit, the club preserved the original wall that stood at the back of the Shed and it remains in place, used to display pictures of Chelsea legends.

Maybe I should declare a certain bias here, too: the food in the press room at the Bridge is the best in the Premier League.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1924 Capacity: 25,194

A trip to Crystal Palace's Selhurst Park is one of the best experiences in the English game

I used to be put off by what I saw, pathetically, as the difficulty of getting to Selhurst Park in south London. Difficult to drive to, hard to find a parking space, not on the Tube, etc, etc.

I got over that some time ago. A trip to Palace is one of the best experiences in the English game.

The atmosphere generated by the Holmesdale Road stand, in particular, makes Selhurst Park one of the best grounds in England to watch football.

Other clubs have seen the volume of their support dim as the demographic of their fans has changed but that has not happened at Selhurst Park. It is one of the few places left that has the power to intimidate and it is all the better for that.

16. MATRADE Loftus Road, Queens Park Rangers

Division: Championship Opened: 1904 Capacity: 18,193

One of the great surviving community grounds, a beautiful, steep-sided gem of a boutique stadium in Shepherd’s Bush, Loftus Road is a place to cherish

One of the great surviving community grounds, a beautiful, steep-sided gem of a boutique stadium in Shepherd’s Bush, Loftus Road is a place to cherish.

When Bernie Ecclestone was a part-owner of the club, I sat in the directors’ box with him a few times and got shushed by Flavio Briatore for talking too much when my neighbour kept asking me questions. That may have been the first time anybody has ever been accused of talking more than Flavio.

The football wasn’t the best during their time there but the hospitality was: they had Mayfair restaurant Cipriani doing the catering.

They are long gone now but the stadium still remains, a wonderful anachronism in a changing world.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1898 Capacity: 30,404

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special - take Nottingham Forest's City Ground for example

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special.

My favourite was always the walk through Queens Gardens in Perth to the WACA. The stroll down from the city centre to the Adelaide Oval is beautiful, too, and the walk along the Thames to Craven Cottage is part of what makes that ground special.

It’s the same with the City Ground. I always park in the same spot, near the River Trent, and walk along the river path until you can see the Forest fans streaming down towards the entrances at the Trent End.

When you get closer, you see the majesty of Trent Bridge next to the City Ground, too, and you feel you’re right at the heart of British sport.

There’s so much history at the City Ground, so much achievement, so much tradition and such a stunning location. It’s a wonderful place to watch a game.

Division: League One Opened: 1901 Capacity: 17,904

Home Park in Plymouth is one of the best football experiences in the league

My affection for Home Park was well entrenched even before I took my seat in the lovely Mayflower Grandstand and watched one of the greatest FA Cup shocks of recent years unfold there in February 2025 when the Pilgrims beat Liverpool.

That was a day to cherish everything about Home Park and the Green Army and the proud local identity enshrined there.

The Mayflower Grandstand, which was renovated recently, remains a beautiful piece of stadium architecture, the staff and stewards are uniformly friendly and welcoming, and the ground occupies a handsome spot in a park on a hill not too far from Plymouth Hoe.

It’s one of the best football experiences in England.

Division: League Two Opened: 1912 Capacity: 15,012

Tranmere Rovers' Prenton Park became a beloved second home for me for a while

Prenton Park became a beloved second home for me for a while. Like Stockport, they used to play their home games on a Friday night for a time and that offered a chance to go and watch them under the lights.

I loved Prenton Park and its sense of community and its noble old stands from the start. When I started work as a trainee on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo in the early 90s, I got to cover Tranmere in the glory days under Johnny King when John Aldridge, who had returned from Real Sociedad, was scoring for fun.

The atmosphere inside the ground on some of those nights on the Wirral was electric. When I was a news reporter at the Echo, I even had to go round to the house of Tranmere’s midfielder Kenny Irons in Norris Green to check out a story.

Kenny had been playing football in his front garden and kicked a ball over a hedge into next door’s garden. His neighbour was an old lady and she wouldn’t give Kenny his ball back. When I pitched up on his doorstep, he saw the funny side.

Division: League Two Opened: 1968 Capacity: 5,278

The Wham Stadium has improved out of all recognition since Andy Holt became involved and any visit to it is a visit to the heart of the difference one man can make to a community

For once, I can turn a blind eye to the renaming of the ground as the Wham Stadium.

That’s because I know how much love and commitment and time and money the Stanley owner, Andy Holt, has put into the resurrection of his local team since he cleared its debts in 2015 when it was on the brink of folding.

Andy doesn’t get much thanks for it and continues to fund the club to the tune of £250,000 a year, despite having claimed he would step down last year. When he does, he will bequeath a lasting legacy in this part of Lancashire.

The ground has improved out of all recognition since he became involved and any visit to it is a visit to the heart of the difference one man can make to a football club and a community. Visionaries like Andy are few and far between in football and the game will be poorer for his absence.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 43,205 (temporarily reduced to 36,887)

Villa Park remains one of the great arenas in the English game, a ground dripping with history

Once one of the great architectural jewels of the English game, Villa Park lost the beauty of Archibald Leitch’s magnificent original Trinity Road Stand in 2000 when it was demolished.

Its loss was a sign of how shabbily we treat the idea of protecting our football heritage in this country.

Despite that, Villa Park remains one of the great arenas in the English game. I stood on the old Holte End in 1983 to see Villa, then European Cup holders, play the mighty Juventus. In October 2024 I was there again when Unai Emery’s side beat Bayern Munich, the team they conquered in the 1982 European Cup final, in their home return to the Champions League.

The atmosphere that night, with the Holte End in full voice, was a wonderful reminder of the great occasions of the past at a ground that feels like stadium aristocracy.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1910 Capacity: 74,244

Old Trafford's iconic Holy Trinity statue stands guard on the forecourt outside the stadium

Old Trafford is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs and memorable nights

Yes, the roof leaks and, yes, Old Trafford could do with a bit of love and attention but there is a magic about this stadium that can never fade. (At least not until Sir Jim Ratcliffe knocks it down and builds the 100,000-seat tourist attraction that is his vision of the football of the future).

Much of that comes from the glories it has witnessed. Sit in the Stretford End and gaze down at a pitch where Duncan Edwards once strode across the turf, George Best danced through the mud and where Bobby Charlton and Denis Law and Bryan Robson and Roy Keane and Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney have played.

It is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs. Outside, on the forecourt, the Holy Trinity statue, a tribute to Best, Charlton and Law, is a place of pilgrimage. As is the Munich Clock, a poignant reminder of the loss of so many of the Busby Babes in 1958.

I was standing on the terraces there when United beat Diego Maradona’s Barcelona 3-0 in the Cup Winners’ Cup in March 1984 and it was one of the best atmospheres I’ve ever felt at an English league ground.

It’s a wonderful place, one of the stadiums that can lay claim to nurturing a chunk of the heart of the English game. They just need a team to be worthy of it again.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 37,645

I love Leeds United's Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit

I love Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road.

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit.

At the other end of the emotional spectrum, fish and chip shops are a decent component of a matchday experience and Graveley's, on Elland Road itself, which has a long queue snaking up to its door from two hours before kick-off, is one of the best football chippies in the country.

The stadium is a proper cathedral of our game, too. One-club cities sometimes generate that kind of passion and it’s evident at Elland Road. I like the fact the stands are named after Don Revie, Norman Hunter, Jack Charlton and John Charles, not an IT company or an airline or a waste management service.

And I love the singing of Marching On Together, a club anthem that dates back more than 50 years, not one of the manufactured club songs you hear at some stadiums these days that mark a cosmetic attempt at authenticity.

You feel the heat of English football at Elland Road, you feel the intensity of it and what it means. At a lot of big clubs, that feeling has been lost. But it's alive here.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1892 Capacity: 52,719

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best

Newcastle are leaning towards building a new stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

Every time I arrive in the city and see St James’ staring down from its vantage point above it, it sends shivers down my spine.

Its position is a symbol of its importance to the city. Inside, it generates one of the best atmospheres in the country, its fans are among the most loyal and the Gallowgate End is one of the most revered sections in our football history.

Newcastle are leaning towards building a new stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t.

7. Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Tottenham Hotspur

Division: Premier League Opened: 2019 Capacity: 62,850

There is an ambition about Spurs' stadium that so many other new-builds lack

Former Spurs chairman Daniel Levy got plenty of criticism for the failures of the club on the pitch but the new stadium still stands as his stunning legacy even now that he has gone

My favourite new stadium anywhere is RB Leipzig’s Red Bull Stadion because of the way it was constructed inside the bowl of the old Zentralstadion but in England, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium stand out.

There is an ambition about Spurs' stadium that so many other new-builds lack, particularly the steepling end behind one of the goals that is said to be modelled on the Yellow Wall at the Westfalenstadion in Dortmund.

I love the nods to the club’s history, particularly the replica of the cockerel that sits above the South Stand and the black and white photos that line the corridors outside the press room.

Former Spurs chairman Daniel Levy got plenty of criticism for the failures of the club on the pitch but the new stadium still stands as his stunning legacy even now that he has gone.

6. Cherry Red Records Stadium, AFC Wimbledon

Division: League One Opened: 2020 Capacity: 9,150

If I lived in London, and Stockport weren't playing, this is where I’d watch my football

I never made it to the old Wimbledon ground at Plough Lane, which is a regret, but I had one of the best of football days when I finally made it to the Cherry Red Records Stadium, near to the site of the old ground, when they played the team that nearly drove them into oblivion, MK Dons, in September 2024.

Just setting foot in this stadium is to feel what it is like to support a team that is at the heart of its community and to be among a fanbase whose team means more to it than just wins and losses.

Love for the game and the team and reverence for the history of the club, the club that was stolen from them and the club they rebuilt, is everywhere, from the kitsch statue of Dave Beasant at the front of the stadium to the illustration on the walls.

It feels like a stadium where everybody knows each other, like neighbours in a street, like a giant, loving, proud family that refuses to be torn apart. The beauty of the architecture here is not in the stadium buildings. It is in the knowledge that this is something built by fans.

If I lived in London, and Stockport weren't playing, this is where I’d watch my football.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1896 Capacity: 27,782

Craven Cottage, home of Fulham, is one of the jewels of English football heritage

Craven Cottage is one of the jewels of English football heritage, and Fulham’s stadium on the banks of the Thames has achieved the difficult task of modernising the ground without losing its character.

The presence of the Cottage, the most glorious eccentricity remaining in our 92 stadiums, in one corner of the ground, is central to that, of course, and helps to make watching a match there so special.

This is a club that has taken care to preserve its history and value a stadium that is different.

Even the walk to the ground through Bishop’s Park and along the path by the river, adds to the pleasure of the experience. It is a joy to visit.

Division: League Two Opened: 1904 Capacity: 8,714

Exeter City have been owned by their supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, they are a shining example of how successful the model can be

I was there last year to see Stockport County play and every away fan got a voucher offering a free cup of tea

It was the summer of 2010 when Exeter City forward Adam Stansfield died of cancer at the age of 31.

‘Stanno’, the father of current Birmingham striker Jay Stansfield, was a hero at the beautiful St James Park stadium, nestled in a nook at the foot of a steep hill and bordered by neat, densely packed terraced streets and a railway cutting.

I drove down there with my elder daughter to look at the tributes to Stansfield and we wandered among the bouquets of flowers and the keepsakes left by heartbroken young fans and the emotional messages that had been left in their thousands on the Big Bank.

It was impossible not to be moved by the profound emotional connection between a city and its club and as the years have passed, St James Park has come to embody for me everything that a football ground should be: full of character and care and camaraderie and community and passion and pride in what it stands for.

I was there last year to see Stockport play and there was a note next to the away turnstile – a turnstile made in another age at the Albion Works in Patricroft – saying: ‘Hatters Fans: Thank you for travelling 474 miles to support your club today.’

Every away fan also got a voucher offering a free cup of tea. The club has been owned by its supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, it is a model of how successful it can be.

The Big Bank has been extended and is now the biggest terrace in English football. So the locals tell me, anyway. There is a club museum, a stall selling farm produce and a supporters’ club bar with big screens.

They built a new stand a few years back, too. It’s called the Adam Stansfield Stand.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2025 Capacity: 52,769

If you are going to move to a new ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium

I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026

I loved Goodison Park and I hated the idea of Everton moving from it. I understand, too, the attitude of some Evertonians who feel the identity of the club will be forever twinned with Goodison.

But if you are going to move to a new ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium. I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026.

I loved everything about it, from its setting on the banks of Mersey, at the heart of the city’s dock culture, which is such a critical component of Liverpool’s heritage, to its vertiginous stands and its community feel.

It still feels like Everton. It doesn’t feel as if the club has been deracinated by its move, as West Ham have been by the change to the London Stadium. Everton now have a stadium that is one of the city’s great landmarks, the first thing visitors to the city see when they sail in on the cruise ships that arrive in Liverpool from all over the world.

Next to the stadium, there still stands the careworn edifice of Victoria Tower, the famous hexagonal clocktower also known as the Dockers’ Clock, that cruise ship passengers used to set their watches to when they arrived from the USA in the city’s boom times. Everton’s home stands proudly beside it now, a symbol of a new Merseyside.

Even more than the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Everton's ground is a standard-bearer for the new generation of English stadiums.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 61,726

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing thanks to fearsome tales about The Kop

Some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't then and it isn’t now

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing.

The tales of The Kop and what they would do to you if they heard your accent were fearsome and when I finally plucked up the courage to go and watch Manchester United play there, I bought a ticket among the home fans and did not speak a word for more than two hours.

But that didn’t stop me being in awe of the place when I first visited. I have never been anywhere like it for the passion and the noise it generated.

Yes, maybe its atmosphere has been slightly diluted by the owners' attempts to attract a new, high-yield breed of casual fan but the ferocity of the emotion the place can still muster can be incredibly moving.

The 2005 Champions League semi-final second leg against Chelsea was probably the noisiest and the most spine-tingling I’ve ever witnessed it although the tie against Barcelona, at the same stage of the competition in 2019, is seared on my brain for similar reasons.

A love for a stadium is about memories, too. My first jobs in journalism were on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo and I spent many wide-eyed afternoons in the old press box at Anfield and in the press conferences afterwards, listening to Kenny Dalglish and, later, Graeme Souness, two of the best British footballers who have ever lived.

Once, on my first visit to the press box, I made the mistake of sitting in Tommy Smith’s seat and was suddenly aware of the hulking presence of the Anfield Iron looming silently above me and a colleague telling me to get up sharpish. I never sat in that seat again.

Some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't and it isn’t. Corporate incursions have altered it but it still has the power to make the hairs on the back of your neck stand on end.

Division: League One Opened: 1891 Capacity: 10,800

I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for Stockport. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92

My family didn’t have any history with Stockport County. I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for them. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

But he was from Heaton Chapel and his grandfather made, and lost, a fortune in the hatting industry in the town in the late 19th century, and he was fiercely proud of Stockport Viaduct and its history and he took me to my first game at Edgeley Park on Monday, April 9, 1979.

We sat in Block A of the Main Stand, now the Danny Bergara Stand, and I breathed in the smell of cigar smoke that drifted up from the man in the sheepskin jacket sitting a couple of rows in front of us and thrilled at the noise coming from the terraces opposite and gazed up to my left at the men working away on their typewriters in the press box, men whose faces I recognised because I had seen their photo bylines in the Manchester Evening News.

I have mentioned elsewhere the curious wonder I felt when people who were strangers to me greeted my dad by name as we walked up the steps to our seats.

I didn’t think my dad had ever been to Edgeley Park before but these people knew him anyway because they were from Stockport and he was from Stockport and those moments made me realise for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community. Not for everyone, but for some of us.

And so even if he wasn’t a fan, I still feel connected to my dad every time I use one of my season tickets, that I bought in a row next to the press box, and gaze over at the place we sat that first time.

I am not a proper fan like the supporters who go week in and week out but I love that ground. I am not a member of any London clubs but Edgeley Park is my club and now, just like my dad, I know people when I go.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

Edgeley Park was where I realised for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community

I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home

Mark Stott has not just invested in the first team and dragged County back up into the Football League but he has bought a new training ground and lavished a lot of love on upgrading facilities for fans in the Cheadle End.

The Danny Bergara Stand still oozes character, it is still similar to the way I remember it from that first game in 1979 and much of the rest of the stadium has been renovated and improved.

I haven’t been so much in recent seasons because I've been spending my spare weekends trying to complete my 92.

I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home.

#1390. Elite players with a terrible penalty record as Lamine Yamal misses another one

Lamine Yamal missed another penalty at the weekend, meaning he has missed more than he has scored this season, but he is not the only elite player with a pretty poor record.

Yamal failed to convert from the spot when Barcelona were trailing 2-0 to Villarreal and even if his blushes were spared thanks to his teammates, it still added to his mixed bag of a penalty record.

Yamal has scored 11 and missed three, giving him a success rate of 79% and here are 10 other elite players who are not so great from the penalty spot.

Messi used to be absolutely awful at penalties. He missed four in the 2014-15 season and did so again in both of the following campaigns. No wonder he tried passing the ball rather than shooting.

Typical of Messi, he clearly identified it as a weakness and worked to improve it. He missed just one a season for the following two campaigns and is now one of the best penalty takers.

His earlier career form does though mean he still makes this list.

Griezmann would choose to have missed 100 penalties if he scored that one in Milan.

The former Atletico man missed a penalty during the Champions League final against city rivals Madrid in the San Siro, a match his team would go on to lose.

Griezmann did at least score in the penalty shootout but could have given Atletico a great chance at victory in the 90 minutes.

That was one of 14 penalties missed in his career to date.

For a player who seemed able to do pretty much whatever he wanted with the ball, Mahrez was oddly poor when it came to penalties.

He’s missed 12 in total, including four for both Leicester and Manchester City.

If you are looking for a player to have missed a penalty for a lot of different clubs, then Edin Dzeko is your man.

He’s missed spot kicks for five clubs and another for his international team, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

He only ever took one for City and missed it before Sergio Aguero resumed duties and his stint at Fenerbahce saves him from a frankly embarrassing record.

He managed to score seven for the Turkish club, missing two, which rescues him somewhat.

Ribery took eight penalties in the 2007-08 season alone but managed to miss two of them.

After that, he was never really given a first-choice run at spot kicks and only took three more for Bayern.

He did have a 100% record for France, though.

The Pro Evo 6 cheat code may have been able to blast them at will from 30 yards but it was not so easy from 12.

He missed a third of the ones he took, of which the majority came whilst he was at Inter.

Had his career ended there, then his penalty record would have been awful but he did redeem himself somewhat with nine scored and one missed for Flamengo in his latter career.

Missing more penalties than you have scored definitely means you are worth including on this list.

Sterling has failed to score six of the 10 penalties he has scored, so no wonder he was taken off penalty duty.

He scored his first-ever penalty back in the 2017-18 season but then missed the next two he took.

Sterling left City with a record of three scored and four missed but was somehow even worse for Chelsea and Arsenal. He took one for each London club and missed both of them.

A 232-goal striker should make for a prolific penalty taker, right? Wrong.

Inzaghi was surprisingly bad from spot kicks, even if he was only given a limited opportunity to take them.

The former Juventus and Milan player only took 25 in his long career and perhaps that is because he missed eight of them.

Most of his misses came from Milan where he scuffed three and managed to score two. No wonder then he took his final penalty nine years before the end of his career.

At one point in his career, Isak was awful at penalties.

When he left Spain for Newcastle in 2022, he had scored six but missed four and since coming to England he has improved a lot.

He missed one in the 2023-24 Premier League season and another in a UEFA Nations League match for Sweden but has scored 13 in the same time period.

His earlier work does mean he has a bad record, for now.

Vinicius Junior took over Cristiano Ronaldo’s number seven shirt but clearly did not inherit his penalty-taking ability.

Of the 20 he has taken, Vinicius has missed six. His most recent came in the 2025/26 Champions League and since then, Kylian Mbappe has been Madrid’s first-choice penalty taker.

Ronaldo, by comparison, has a conversion record of 83%.

#1388. 8 naff football-related presents you could get this Christmas: Soap, Cards, Monopoly…

It’s getting close to that time of year when your relatives know you like football and so try their best to get a gift, but they don’t always quite get it right.

Liking football means you often get just about anything as a gift provided it has your club’s badge on it (if you’re lucky) and let’s all hope that none of us open any of these under the tree this year.

Here are eight wonderfully awful football-related Christmas gifts for this year.

When we heard Bristol City were selling grass we thought that’s one way to raise the transfer budget but turns out it is of the turf variety.

The Robins are releasing soap that has been “scientifically” made to replicate the smell of the pitch at Ashton Gate so you can shower with the smell of a pitch that is 18th in the Championship currently.

We will give them credit for the excellent slogan of “because you’re turf it” but it has naturally opened them to such jokes as it smelling like the s**t football that gets played on it.

Profits will at least go to the club’s foundation.

Introducing the Ashton Gate-scented soap to raise funds for the Robins Foundation’s work in communities across Bristol.

Available online and in-store. https://t.co/kbDyZ1XbTC

— Bristol City FC (@BristolCity) November 24, 2026

Ipswich are selling a Christmas candle called Ipswicks which they describe as a Luxury Scented Christmas Candle smelling of Pine, Eucalyptus & Cedarwood.

We don’t know what the Ipswich marketing department thinks of their fans though as there is a warning to not touch the tin as it may get hot.

Club-branded playing cards is not that unusual but we are including these because Arsenal have decided to charge their fans £70 for three packs of cards.

For that money, you get a commemorative box that has the names of the players that won the title last season and the cards are in the colours of the kits used last campaign but we hope no one buys that because that is an incredible waste of money.

Just imagine, you’ve had your Christmas dinner and someone suggests some card games and then pulls those out. Awful.

If you think £70 is too much, then don’t worry, you can get a single pack of cards for £18.

Honestly, there are so many things from the United store that could have made the list. Firstly, they are selling quite literally a cardboard box for £10. They also have a sack so the jokes write themselves.

But the one item we have picked out is the United-branded Monopoly board they are selling for £50.

Realising that there are not 28 United-related places to go on a Monopoly board, the club decided to name each square after moments in their history, fair enough. What isn’t fair enough is that the final square, which is the most expensive slot on the board, comes with the title of “2016/17 WON THE LOT.”

Sorry? We’ve checked the league table and can’t help but see you were sixth? And surely the FA have made a mistake because they seem to think that Arsenal won the cup that year? While we are at it, you will want to have a word with UEFA because they seem to think that Real Madrid won the Champions League that season.

“The lot” United are referring to is actually the League Cup, Europa League and Community Shield. Did Jose Mourinho commission this?

Well they’ve got to pay their massive wages somehow.

Man Utd truly shocking in 2026-27 Premier League wage bill vs. position comparison

It may have slipped your attention but did you know that League Two side Northampton Town are now owned by a Brazilian consortium fronted by Alexandre Pato?

The Cobblers are doing their best to spread the word by releasing a number of Brazil-inspired pieces of merchandise and so we are picking the half and half scarf that has Northampton in the middle and the Brazil flag on the ends.

It feels like the kind of thing that will end up in the National Football Museum in 100 years’ time.

The problem with football is that it is fast-moving and so one product that is good one year can quickly become out of date. Step forward Arne Slot figure.

Liverpool commissioned a set of Soccerstarz of the 2025/26 squad but, unfortunately for Slot, is still hanging around in a storage cupboard somewhere.

They are trying their best to shift it, reducing it down to £1 or 90p if you are a club member, but even he looks annoyed at still being there.

Do you even love your club if you don’t wear socks promoting the club’s owners?

Any Leicester fans afraid of being called a plastic ought to buy themselves a pair of these fetching purple socks that do not display really anything to do with the club but instead the brand of King Power.

There is a Leicester badge but it is on the sole of the foot meaning no one will see it but at least you show off your favourite Bangkok-based travel retail conglomerate.

Bonus points to the Foxes for the Sonic the Hedgehog scarf. We don’t know why either.

It’s late on Christmas Day. You’re full to the brim but excited for the day’s football tomorrow.

You fancy a little tipple to round off the festivities and so what better way to scratch that itch and get prepared for tomorrow than with a Sheffield United shot glass with a picture of a chip butty on the side of it?

For just £3.50, or you can pay in four interest-free payments of 87p, you can have a shot glass which is “a nod to the no-fuss, unpretentious spirit that runs through every corner of S2 [where Bramall Lane is].

Apparently it “carries the kind of quiet pride that doesn’t need to shout” but it just makes us feel rather queasy.

#1387. A new view of Amazonian leaf seasonality

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gerbrand Koren is at the Copernicus Institute of Sustainable Development, Utrecht University, 3584 CB Utrecht, the Netherlands.

The Amazon rainforest plays a key part in the cycling of carbon and water on regional and global scales, and is widely viewed as a perennially evergreen ecosystem. However, writing in Nature, Song et al.1 report that there are extended periods when trees in most of the rainforest remain leafless. Known as deciduousness, this state occurs between the shedding of old leaves and the emergence and early development (flushing) of fresh ones. The authors also found that hydroclimatic conditions such as annual rainfall have a more crucial role in determining this pattern of leaf behaviour than do soil properties and light availability. The seasonal variation in tropical leaf cover and photosynthetic activity in the Amazon observed by the authors is less pronounced than that seen for broadleaf trees in temperate and boreal climate zones.

#1386. Michael Carrick will not survive unless Manchester United change

Sometimes comments, however over the top, hit home. Michael Carrick will desperately hope the remark from his former Manchester United team-mate Gary Neville is not one of them. That it does not stick. That it does not come to define his time in charge of United this season – if he lasts this season. Or be used in one of those highlight reels, with doom-laden music, to explain the story of this Premier League campaign.

On TV co-commentary duty for Sky, Neville referred to United as “blue mannequins” (they were wearing their away kit) and said that for a period after half-time it was the worst he had ever seen them play since he started watching, aged five. Neville is now 51. That is a lot of games to settle on this conclusion so strongly and, surely, inaccurately.

"They were absolutely mannequins!" Gary Neville says Michael Carrick has to stop defending the Manchester United players. pic.twitter.com/Pa4PqIoRbh

But so passive was their football that is the way he felt in the moment. For a club with United’s “attack, attack, attack” tradition – becoming something of a distant memory as seasons pass – that is a damning as it gets.

Neville’s Sky paymasters will be delighted by his emotive, insulting, headline-grabbing language. But he of course exaggerated a point to make a point. United, and Carrick, were, indeed, far too passive, lacking aggression, urgency and belief. They just do not press. United did, for too long, play like a team of dummies.

Against Fulham they almost played walking football until they conceded, desperation kicked in and they chased the game to salvage a late draw.

It begs the question: what is Carrick doing with this team? Yes, he may have been let down by no defensive signings in the summer – even if he must have bought into the plan to prioritise a midfield rebuild – but he is far from absolved from blame.He will cling to the response to Lisandro Martínez’s own goal, to striking a post twice in the first half from Matheus Cunha and Bruno Fernandes, to managing to avoid a third successive defeat in a week, which would have led to the crisis klaxon being sounded. Carrick can talk about how ridiculous it would be to question his position as head coach. But is it?

We now go into a three-week international break and the Premier League vacuum would have been filled by a debate over Carrick’s future, whether he is up to the job and another existential examination as to where United are heading. And who is to blame.

That still might happen. United did not lose. But they were not remotely good enough, as has been the case for most of the season. Their only league win in five was against newly promoted Ipswich Town, having lost to newly promoted Hull City. They have also drawn at Everton and now at Fulham, who started the day bottom of the table and remain winless. Apart from facing Manchester City, it has hardly been the most taxing of starts. Except they are down in 12th and have not played well at all.

It is not just that. Last year, United revamped their attack. Benjamin Sesko was absent through injury but are Cunha – despite his goal – Bryan Mbeumo and Marcus Rashford actually showing they are good enough? They, too, are passive and do not effect the play. Do not have that killer instinct. There is then an over-reliance on Fernandes. And if he does not do it, then who steps up?

That 15 minutes after half-time that culminated in the Martínez mishap was certainly woeful. But despite going close, United were also second best in the opening period, with Fulham’s 19-year-old academy product Josh King showing why he was so close to a senior England call-up. The forward ran riot, tormenting left-back Luke Shaw and was only denied by Senne Lammens. On more than one occasion, especially with a smart save with his right boot.

The goalkeeper was at the centre of Fulham’s goal, which was a shambles that summed up the state of United, who are just too easy to play against. And, so, Fulham’s captain Calvin Bassey was too strong for Cunha, who threw himself to the ground, looking for a foul, losing the ball from Kobbie Mainoo’s easy pass. The defender strode forward before Lammens parried his low shot, which then bounced off Martínez and back past the goalkeeper and into the net.

It was a Hammersmith End House of Horrors for United. To cap it all, Martínez then tried to blame Lammens who had, frankly, kept United in the game up until that point and could legitimately have told him where to go. And asked why he could not trap a ball and clear.

"A horror at the Hammersmith end!"Lisandro Martínez puts the ball into his own net and Fulham lead! 😯 pic.twitter.com/jDmY4zL2XN

Fulham will certainly feel their own frustration. But with their new head coach Álvaro Arbeloa and an evolving team – if only striker Gonzalo García was more deadly – there are clear signs of optimism, having also just drawn at Liverpool.

United’s late equaliser was fortunate. Yes, they applied pressure but to no real effect until Cunha’s shot deflected off the boot of Fulham defender David Affengruber as he tried to block, to wrong-foot goalkeeper Bernd Leno, who had also been outstanding. It was credited to Cunha, his first of the season, and the relief from Carrick was understandably palpable.

Manchester United are LEVEL! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/DCxwlrzf1M

But, once again, it was not up to the standard needed. And beyond the point, beyond the avoidance of defeat, that is the reality of where United are right now under Carrick who needs to step up, take more responsibility. And, like his team, be far less passive. Otherwise, he will not last.

Might these games offer less possession and more counter-attacking chances? That’s glass half full.

I was purely referring to the fact that they walked around the pitch. I’ve never seen a Manchester United team walk around on the pitch that much.

Michael has got to stop defending them. I get why he wants to defend them, he’s loyal, and there’s a long way to go into the season.

Both teams were the same, I called them mannequins. I’ve never seen United walk around so much out of possession, no alertness, no being on your toes.

I wish he could play those attacking players, but they are going to kill him defensively.

Neville goes on to call that period: “An absolute disgrace, nowhere near good enough.”

"They were absolutely mannequins!" Gary Neville says Michael Carrick has to stop defending the Manchester United players. pic.twitter.com/Pa4PqIoRbh

I know Manchester United have a lot of individual quality, I have played against them for many years and know them really well. I know to be alert in case they shoot from distance. When you make some saves in the game you feel very focused. Unfortunately I couldn’t keep out the goal but that is football.

I didn’t think we were. Did you think we were? Football is a difficult game. We controlled a lot of the first half. It’s the Premier League and you will have spells where you don’t have it all your own way. To expect total dominance for the whole game, I don’t think anyone gets that in this league.

I thought we should have won the game, I thought we created enough to win the game. The goal we did concede is one of them goals. The boys could have thought it is one of those days but I really like the reaction. We nearly won it in the end. We came to get the win of course, the way it panned out and the way we finished is the positive we take from it.

I think we did a good game. Obviously not an easy game for us, we were in the bottom position but we saw personality with the ball, we were brave. We had moments where we had to defend but in general we did a good game.

We wanted to control the transition and the counter attacks. We know they put too many people inside so we have to control the space behind our midfielders. They sometimes found the spaces, it is a difficult match against a big team and for me they will be near the top of the league by the end of the season.

Now we have to find the first victory. If you see our first five games we have already played Man Utd, Chelsea, at Anfield, at Sunderland. Now we have an October that will be so important for us.

There were so many things for them, you can see it in the foul by [Harry] Maguire. Every decision was for them. I knew after the game against Manchester City that they don’t like Manchester United to lose.

It’s hard to explain, I feel after the first half we always get a lot of chances and create, play well.

In the beginning of the second half they put in more energy than us and we cannot accept this. We always play better after conceding goal, and it cannot be like this.

I don’t think today was about final decisions, we were a bit unlucky, I hit the post, and Bruno hit the post. We need to create more and hope the luck comes and we score. We need to improve in every single position.

It was too slow, Fulham ran more and looked like they wanted to win more. Bassey just eased Cunha out the way [for Fulham’s goal] and looked like he wanted to take the game to Man United and Carrick will be thinking ‘we need to do a lot more’.

It was a game that was a real struggle for both teams. Both lacked confidence. There were challenges for both managers coming into this game, they both need the international break to start their seasons again.

The defensive work from both teams was awful and lacked effort. Carrick will be relieved going back to Manchester with a goal and a point.

Manchester United play Spurs when the Premier League returns in three weeks, in a game that will feel huge.

5 - With five points, this is Manchester United's joint-lowest tally after five games of a Premier League season, also picking up five in 2014-15.Sluggish. pic.twitter.com/UZTBWRpGnm

Fulham remain winless but the draw lifts them above Spurs, who will spend the international break at the foot of the table. It is just one win in five for United, and it was another performance which was far from convincing. It could have been worse though, they were a few minutes away from losing. On this evidence, both of these teams are in for a struggle relative to expectations.

Fulham wanted a free-kick on the edge of the box for a sliding challenge on Kevin for Maguire but the referee decides he got the ball.

United break forward and win a corner. It comes for Martinez who shifts his feet to shoot with his right foot and the goal-bound effort was blocked!

Just the three minutes of added time to play, but United are the team pushing forward searching for an unlikely winner.

United may have just spared themselves a damaging defeat, and there might just be time to go on an win this. Cunha with a speculative shot from outside the box, and Affengruber extends his left leg to block the shot but the deflection leaves Leno stranded. A stroke of luck for United but Fulham have invited it.

Manchester United are LEVEL! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/DCxwlrzf1M

Bassey now penalised for a high boot on Dalot, United free-kick on the halfway line. Fulham just about standing firm, and they are helped when a crossfield pass towards Dorgu bounces off for a throw-in.

United with another corner and there are loud appeals for a handball penalty against Bassey, the proximity was very close but his hand was up. But VAR takes a look and the fact the hand was tucked in towards his chest spares the Fulham defender.

Fulham and the home crowd happy with a goal kick after an overhit cross towards Shaw at the back post. Dorgu has been sent on in Carrick’s last throw of the dice, replacing Shaw at left-back.

You would not say United are pulling Fulham from pillar to post, it feels a little hopeful, but it is one-way traffic. An attack against defence session in Fulham’s half. Charles and Kevin do well to relieve the pressure momentarily, but United are back on the attack again.

Here are those changes: Mason Mount on for Kobbie Mainoo for United, while Andersen replaces King for the home team. Arbeloa happy to hold what he has. Lisandro Martinez volleys a shot over the bar.

Positive first involvement from Zirkzee, releasing Mbeumo, but the Fulham defenders read his intentions and blocked the shot after he cut inside. Joachim Andersen is preparing to come on for Fulham, as is Mason Mount for United.

Much better from Fulham, another attack started by Bassey reading play just like the goal, but this time Lammens’s wrists were strong to parry Kevin’s shot. Rashford is then flagged offside.

Fulham change: Larsson is on for Berge, Sweden for Norway. And Carrick has brought on Zirkzee for Rashford. Famous last words, but does that make you more likely to score a goal? Not that Rashford can feel hard done to.

Fulham have stopped playing since they scored, and they needed Leno again to tip a Cunha shot around the post. The United forward was falling over, but he generated enough power to trouble the goalkeeper. From the corner, Maguire picks up the ball on the far side and chips a cross over the blue shirts in the middle.

Kevin sold himself in a one-on-one with Rashford, but King did well to put his foot in at the edge of the box and the ball bounces through kindly to Leno. Tielemans then misplaces a pass when United were in a promising position.

If United had played like this from the start of the second half they would not be losing, but now they have just 20 minutes plus stoppage time to overturn the deficit.

Fulham making a double sub: Kevin and Palacios on for Iwobi and Bobb.

United have roused themselves since conceding, winning a flurry of corners.

What a save from Leno! Mbeumo’s curling shot from outside the box was arcing beautifully into the far corner, but the German goalkeeper tipped his effort around the post.

Then Maguire is eased out at the back post, and Fulham breathe a sigh of relief.

Strong words from Gary Neville after the goal went it: “I’ve watched United since the age of five and that is the worst 15 minutes [from half-time to the goal] I have seen them play.”

Well doesn’t that just sum up United’s season so far. There are appeals for a foul on Cunha from Bassey, but the Fulham defender was stronger and he took some initiative to drive towards the box. Bassey let fly and kept his shot down, Lammens could only stick out a leg and the ball rebounded off the helpless Martinez and back into the net.

"A horror at the Hammersmith end!"Lisandro Martínez puts the ball into his own net and Fulham lead! 😯 pic.twitter.com/jDmY4zL2XN

Fulham have a corner after it opened up nicely for Iwobi at the edge of the box, but his left-footed strike deflects behind. A very smooth footballer, but finishing has never been Iwobi’s strong suit. Fulham fail to make anything of the corner.

Fulham and United’s fans now urging their teams on after the game halted to glacial pace. Nothing much happening at all since the start of the second half.

Gary Neville growing increasingly frustrated by the lack of intensity out of possession by both teams: “Never walk on a football pitch.” Questions have been asked of United’s fitness levels and physical readiness for the new season. Fulham enjoying a spell of possession in United’s half again.

More from Neville: “It’s like it’s time for the whites to play against the blue mannequins, before they reverse it up the other end. One thing I do know, I’ve played in a lot of football matches, it’s not right.”

There has been a real lack of conviction in Rashford’s play in the final third, this time it was underhit pass across the box towards Mbeumo which was cut out. Good ball by Tielemans to release Rashford, but no end product again.

Sir Alex Ferguson is watching on at Craven Cottage. The game has slipped into one of its lulls again.

Nice football from Fulham involving Charles and Iwobi but United break forward after a loose touch by Bobb. Fernandes did well to keep the ball and wait for support, and Castagne is booked for a block on Rashford.

The first few minutes of the half are played deep in Fulham’s territory, but United’s delivery from wide is not good enough and Cunha is penalised for a foul in the middle in any case.

At half-time that is another worrying performance from Manchester United. Yes, they could be ahead and have created chances, with Bruno Fernandes hitting the post. But on the balance of play they should be behind with Fulham’s 19-year-old Josh King the best player on the pitch and United reliant on goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Michael Carrick has more work to do during the interval than Fulham’s Alvaro Arbeloa and cannot be happy with how defensively vulnerable his team and but also how wasteful they are in front of goal.

Both teams will believe they should have scored in that first half in a game that has oscillated between periods of passivity and flurries of goal-mouth action. When United speed up their interplay, it looks like they can cut through Fulham, but Carrick’s team’s box defending leaves much to be desired. There were 26 shots on goal without reward in that 45 minutes.

Another chance is missed, this time Rashford with a side foot over the bar from a Cunha cross that took a nick on the way through. Always leaning back, poor technique from a player of his standing.

Fulham then throw a punch back, but King is booked for diving after pushing the ball beyond Maguire. The attacker is not happy, but not sure he can have any complaints.

United almost caught out by a one-two between Iwobi and Garcia, but Lammens rushes off his line to get there first. Both attacks look to have the beating of both defences, but somehow there have been no goals.

United’s best move of the game, starting with a whipped pass from Tielemans when under pressure into Dalot who turns into space inside. Fernandes could have taken a shot on himself from the edge of the box, but he moved the ball on to Rashford but his side-foot shot was tame and straight at Leno.

The game has settled after that flurry of chances when both teams could easily have scored. Fulham do well to block Rashford’s sight of goal as he cuts inside looking for a shot, and then Mbeumo commits a foul.

Cunha with a deflected strike from distance, which arcs over Leno and glances off the post! The sort of deflection that gives a goalkeeper no chance, Leno was scrambling.

Mainoo’s shot is blocked from the corner, and then Fulham break forward with numbers. Iwobi picks out Josh King in the box, and Lammens sticks out a right leg to keep out his driven shot.

Josh King is again showing why he was so close to a full England call-up. The 19-year-old is at the heart of the action as Fulham continue to create chance after chance against a very shaky Manchester United defence who have been reliant on goalkeeper Senne Lammens.

Fulham respond, with Robinson’s cross looping to the back post to the unmarked King but he could not get over the side-foot volley and it was a comfortable save from Lammens.

This stop was less comfortable though: Lammens plunges to his right to keep out a dig by Sander Berge from the edge of the box. It came after Garcia kicked fresh air in the area.

Then Bobb collects the ball in space at the edge of the box and is able to turn but he dragged his shot wide.

The home team and crowd have burst into life.

Fernandes hits the post for United! He should score, and it was poor defending from Fulham. Affengruber ran beyond the ball and was rolled by Cunha who was able to drive into the box, and he pulled the ball back for Fernandes who dragged his shot a touch, and it rebounded off the foot of the post.

Bruno Fernandes hits the post! 😬 pic.twitter.com/jMzn8ZyoYa

Better from United, turning the screw around the Fulham box but neither Mainoo nor Rashford fashion room for a shot, and then Dalot shoots wide from 25 yards with his weaker left foot.

Josh King finding space off the shoulder of United’s midfield again, but his shot from a tight angle is always rising. United are asking for trouble though if Fulham’s most creative player keeps collecting the ball in those spaces

United then come forward, with Robinson selling himself against Mbeumo, but Rashford cannot get over the header at the back post.

Fulham with a smooth passage of play from deep, finding space down United’s right and Garcia had made a dangerous run between Maguire and Martinez. Iwobi looked for his team-mate, but the ball glanced off his foot as he tried to direct it towards goal.

The interesting thing about Manchester United’s attack is that while they are all, clearly, individually good players do they actually do enough to warrant their status at the club? The truth is Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Marcus Rashford simply have to do more and dominate games. We are yet to see that form them this season and, apart from Lisandro Martinez forcing a fine save from Bernd Leno, Fulham have carried the greater threat here.

Fulham have a corner after Josh King used his body well against Shaw. There has been lots of cat and mouse so far, both teams trying to play patiently from deep and the out of possession team lying in wait for a mistake. United clear the Fulham corner.

Bassey defends well in the area, but United are starting to warm to their task. Tielemans lifts a dangerous cross into the box, and Fernandes’s header deflects off Affengruber and behind for a corner.

A short corner comes to nothing, but from a second or possibly third phase Lisandro Martinez lets fly from distance with a swerving, outside of the left foot shot. Appeared destined for the corner, but Leno pushed the ball around the post. Great try from Martinez.

United have settled on the ball now, enjoying some possession of their own in non-threatening areas. Neither team appears too interested in gambling on the high press, a degree of wariness in their approaches. That was a nice Fulham move, sweeping from right to left, but Iwobi chipped a cross into Lammens’s gloves. Tielemans then looks for the run of Rashford with a through ball, but the forward is offside. Plenty of green grass behind Fulham’s back four though.

Fulham move the ball well again, Robinson setting the ball back for Garcia to strike from just outside the box but he dragged his shot wide of the near post. Too much time and space for the forward if you are United inclined, though. Tielemans then passes the ball out of play, splitting the difference between Dalot and Mbeumo.

Promising signs for Josh King as he carries the ball from the right touchline into a dangerous central position, unchallenged by United’s midfield. The home team have monopolised the ball so far, United sitting off in a shape, perhaps waiting for an error and the chance to counter-attack.

United get the game under way at Craven Cottage.

Very difficult to predict what you are going to be served by either of these teams. Both of their seasons are on a knife edge even at the this early juncture.

If Manchester United could choose a Premier League away fixture to revitalise their season, Fulham would be it. Not just because they are bottom of the league with just one point, albeit impressively earned last week away to Liverpool, but because United have not been beaten at Craven Cottage since December 2009 – although, not such a good omen for United, is the fact that Michael Carrick was in their team that day (playing at centre-back).

Michael Carrick dismissed as “ridiculous” any suggestion that his job as Manchester United’s head coach was at risk this early in the season. But he needs a positive result today against Fulham otherwise much of the prolonged international break will be taken up by debate as to whether he is up to it. United do not play again after today until they host stricken Tottenham Hotspur on October 10 and their start to this season has simply not been good enough. The concern for Carrick appears his inability to positively affect games when things are going against United.

JJ Gabriel has been in the news this week, and Sam Wallace writes in his column this week that the battle to sign up and coming academy players is growing ever more fierce between Premier League clubs. Managers are handing out debuts earlier and earlier to satisfy the demands of the best young players, and an increasing number of clubs are happy to gamble significant fees and wages on potental.

Fulham starting XI: Leno, Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson, Berge, Charles, King, Bobb, Iwobi, Garcia

Subs: Lecomte, Andersen, Palacios, Muniz, Kevin, Larsson, Manuel Angel, Sessegnon. Smith Rowe

Here's how The Fulham shape up. ⚪️ pic.twitter.com/0IxS0J3ldf

United starting XI: Lammens, Dalot, Martinez, Maguire, Shaw, Mainoo, Tielemans, Fernandes, Mbeumo, Cunha, Rashford

Subs: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Zirkzee, Dorgu, Yoro, Andrey Santos, Heaven, Baleba, Lacey.

Presenting your United XI to face Fulham ✊

The script pretty much writes itself these days. A flicker of optimism and hope of a fresh start giving way to the same old frustrations, complaints and inquests, the cumulative toll of which places an ever greater strain on a club mired in mediocrity but with little reprieve from the expectations that come with bearing such an illustrious name.

Michael Carrick says Pro Ref’s apology over the derby fiasco means little to Manchester United – but warned his players they cannot allow such setbacks to derail their season.

Chief refereeing officer Howard Webb formally apologised to United after the VAR officials Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus failed to spot Enzo Fernandez was offside before wrongly allowing Erling Haaland’s winning goal to stand in Manchester City’s 1-0 victory at Old Trafford.

United were left shocked by the scale of the blunder, which came with 30 minutes of the game remaining and City already down to 10 men.

But Carrick has told his players not to become preoccupied with such injustices as they bid to overcome their poor start to the season before a crucial trip to Craven Cottage.

“It can have an impact in the moment of time, it can have a big impact, but we can’t let it have an impact on the rest of the season,” the United manager said.

“That’s for us to get back to winning ways as soon as possible. Listen, one-off things can happen, at the time it was a pretty big one, we know that. I don’t think I need to go over that.

“But yeah, I’ve got faith in it [VAR], it’s the system that we work towards and that we use so the apology doesn’t mean an awful lot.”

Carrick added: “I can appreciate and I respect it for them putting their hands up and saying we got that wrong, I think it happens - it does happen.

“But moving forward, yeah, we just have to deal with it, what’s thrown in front of us. And maybe we get one or two decisions on the back of how it balances out - percentages or law of averages or whatever that may be.

“But that was a pretty big one to take and had a huge impact on that game and that’s why it was particularly tough.”

Michael Carrick may have had a point when he said it was “ridiculous” to question his future this early in the season, but this afternoon’s game at Fulham will shape the mood at Manchester United for the next three weeks.

A tally of four points from their first four games of the season is a disappointing start, and Brighton added to the sense of gloom in the League Cup by becoming the first side in 50 years to win from 2-0 down at Old Trafford.

With Champions League football on the agenda, that competition was at the bottom of United’s priority list but the ragged nature of the performance prompted boos around the stadium.

The no-show at Hull and defeat to 10-man City also fall into the “it’s how you lose” category of defeat, while there are widening fissures between the fanbase and the club’s hierarchy over ticketing policy and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s political interventions.

The mood has also been sour at Fulham in the first few weeks of the season. In fact, they start the game bottom of the Premier League with one point, but do have the incentive of knowing a draw would take them above Spurs.

Following reports of friction between some established players and new head coach Alvaro Arbeloa though, they produced their best performance of the season in a goalless draw at Anfield last week when they had chances to win the game.

Fulham made nine changes in the League Cup in mid-week, but still ran out 3-2 winners at West Ham. Despite the west London club being an established mid-table Premier League team for a number of seasons, and United’s vulnerable state for the past few years, Fulham have beaten their opponent’s just once in the league since December 2009.Full team news on the way shortly.

#1385. Zohran Mamdani hobbles into City Hall wearing walking boot after suffering gruesome injury in soccer game

Published: 15:41 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 23:53 EST, 20 November 2026

Zohran Mamdani squared off with New York media and now the city's mayor will need a few months to recover.

As he revealed Friday while announcing plans to replace Rikers Island jail, Mamdani was playing in a soccer match against the local press corps at an indoor pitch in lower Manhattan when he tore his right Achilles tendon. Consequently, Mamdani is now using crutches and a walking boot, which he expects to be in for the next six to eight weeks.

'I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch and I forgot that I was 35,' Mamdani told gathered media on Friday at City Hall, where he was forced to rely on crutches.

Mamdani hopes to be back playing soccer again in nine months.

Local media may not be to blame here. As Mamdani told the New York Post, he arrived late to the game and began playing without properly stretching. What's more, the Post reported that Mamdani was overheard asking his police guards which reporter tackled him, only to be told he went down untouched.

Despite Mamdani's injury, team City Hall beat the local media, 8-4.

As he revealed Friday while announcing plans to close Rikers Island, Mamdani was playing  against the local press corps when tore his Achilles. Now he's in a boot (pictured)

Zohran Mamdani and wife Rama Duwaji are seen during a Brazil-Morocco World Cup match

Born in Uganda and raised in Manhattan's Morningside Heights neighborhood, Mamdani played cricket and soccer in his youth. He even suited up for Bowdoin College's JV team during his days at the Maine school. Then later, as an adult, he became a shareholder of Spanish second-division club Real Oviedo.

But his biggest impact on the sport came over the summer, when New York welcomed thousands of tourists for the World Cup action at MetLife Stadium in nearby East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Upset with ticket prices for the matches, Mamdani organized more than 100 free watch parties around the city. The events were well attended and helped locals engage with the tournament even though no actual matches were played in New York.

Zohran Mamdani, center, joined by, from left, United States soccer star Tim Weah NYC World Cup Czar Maya Handa, and New York council member Yusef Salaam back in May

'We said from the beginning that the World Cup belongs to New Yorkers. This summer, we proved it,' Mamdani said in a statement. 'In the most international city on earth, you didn't need thousands of dollars to be part of the world's game.

'A kid in Corona, a nurse in Bay Ridge and a small business owner in Little Haiti could all celebrate together — for free or at a price they could afford,' he continued. 'That's what we mean when we talk about a city for the many.

'This summer, strangers became neighbors on Open Streets and in free Fan Fests across the city because government made room for people to come together. And long after the confetti is swept away, New Yorkers will keep what we built: safer streets, faster buses, stronger protections, closer neighbors and the memory of a summer when the whole world felt at home here.'
